concepts.title: Theme, Style & Context
concepts.intro: seaborn wraps matplotlib to apply consistent themes. set_theme() is the modern single entry point. style controls axes appearance; context controls scale (paper→poster).
concepts.explanation: `sns.set_theme()` is seaborn's single switch for figure-wide look and feel. It wraps the three older calls — `set_style()`, `set_context()` and `set_palette()` — into one, and applies them to **global** matplotlib state (`matplotlib.rcParams`). That is why it returns nothing: every figure created *afterwards* inherits the theme. `style` picks the axes look (`'darkgrid'`, `'whitegrid'`, `'dark'`, `'white'`, `'ticks'`); `context` rescales fonts and lines for the display medium, from `'paper'` (smallest) through `'notebook'`, `'talk'` up to `'poster'` (largest); `font_scale` multiplies font sizes on top of that. The `rc` dict is the escape hatch: any matplotlib rcParam can be pinned, e.g. `rc={'lines.linewidth': 2.5}` — and rc entries win over whatever style and context already chose. Because theming is global, state leaks easily between figures: use `sns.axes_style(...)` / `sns.plotting_context(...)` as context managers for temporary changes, and `sns.reset_defaults()` (back to seaborn defaults) or `sns.reset_orig()` (back to matplotlib factory settings) to clean up. The gotcha that bites most often: `set_theme()` must run *before* `plt.subplots()`, because figure size and font rcParams are read at artist-creation time. The exercises below have you build a themed line chart and prove that rc overrides really landed on the produced figure.
keyPoints: `sns.set_theme(style=..., context=..., palette=..., font_scale=..., rc=...)` is the modern one-call replacement for `set_style` + `set_context` + `set_palette`.
`style` controls axes appearance (`darkgrid`, `whitegrid`, `dark`, `white`, `ticks`); `context` (`paper` < `notebook` < `talk` < `poster`) scales every font and line for the medium.
The `rc` dict is applied *after* style and context — `rc={'figure.figsize': (7.0, 4.5)}` makes every later bare `plt.subplots()` produce a 7.0×4.5 inch figure.
`set_theme()` mutates global matplotlib state and returns `None`; call it before creating figures, since rcParams are read when artists are created.
`sns.axes_style()` / `sns.plotting_context()` read the current style (or set it temporarily via `with`); `sns.reset_orig()` restores matplotlib factory defaults.

blocks.title: set_theme / set_style / set_context / axes_style / plotting_context
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# ── set_theme() — modern all-in-one ───────────────────────────────────
sns.set_theme(
    style="darkgrid",       # "darkgrid" "whitegrid" "dark" "white" "ticks"
    palette="deep",         # see color_palette() section for all options
    context="notebook",     # "paper" "notebook" "talk" "poster"
    font="DejaVu Sans",
    font_scale=1.0,         # multiply all font sizes
    rc={"lines.linewidth":1.5},  # arbitrary rcParams overrides
)

# ── style options ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# "darkgrid"  — gray background with grid (default for EDA)
# "whitegrid" — white background with grid (good for printed figures)
# "dark"      — gray background without grid
# "white"     — clean white background
# "ticks"     — white with tick marks on axes

# ── context scale factors ══════════════════════════════════════════
# "paper"    — smallest (0.8× default) for multi-panel figures
# "notebook" — default (1×)
# "talk"     — larger (1.3×) for presentations
# "poster"   — largest (1.6×) for posters/walls

# Context as context manager (temporary)
with sns.plotting_context("talk"):
    fig,ax=plt.subplots()
    ax.plot([1,2,3],[1,4,9])
    plt.close()

# Style as context manager
with sns.axes_style("whitegrid"):
    fig,ax=plt.subplots()
    ax.plot([1,2,3],[1,4,9])
    plt.close()

# Reset to matplotlib defaults
sns.reset_defaults()
sns.reset_orig()   # even more thorough reset

print("Theme/style/context documented")

concepts.title: Relational & Distribution Plots
concepts.intro: relplot() and displot() are figure-level wrappers that create FacetGrids. scatterplot/lineplot/histplot/kdeplot are axes-level equivalents.
concepts.explanation: seaborn splits its plotting API in two. **Axes-level** functions — `scatterplot`, `lineplot`, `histplot`, `kdeplot`, `ecdfplot` — draw onto an existing matplotlib Axes (pass `ax=`) and return that Axes. **Figure-level** wrappers — `relplot`, `displot` — build their own figure and return a `FacetGrid` whose `.figure` attribute holds the canvas; they can facet with `col=`/`row=`. The single biggest `lineplot` gotcha: it is an *estimator* plot. If several rows share the same `x`, seaborn groups them, applies `estimator` (default `'mean'`) and surrounds the line with an uncertainty band (`errorbar=('ci', 95)` by default; `errorbar=None` removes it — the old `ci=` parameter is deprecated). With unique `x` values you get the raw series and a single `ax.lines[0]`. `scatterplot` maps every row to a point in one collection — `ax.collections[0].get_offsets()` returns the (x, y) pairs — while `hue`, `size` and `style` add visual dimensions plus a legend without creating more collections. `histplot` bins the data: pass `bins=[e0, e1, ...]` for exact edges (bins are half-open `[ei, ei+1)` — an edge value falls into the bin to its right — except the last bin, which closes on the right), `stat=` to rescale bar heights, and `multiple='stack'` to pile `hue` levels on top of each other. `kdeplot` smooths the same data into a density curve (`bw_adjust`, `fill`, `levels`). The exercises below pin these behaviors down with assertions you can verify on the returned Axes.
keyPoints: `lineplot` aggregates: repeated `x` values collapse to `estimator='mean'` and gain an error band; unique `x` values give you the raw series in `ax.lines[0]`.
`errorbar=None` replaces the deprecated `ci=None`; the band lives in `ax.collections`, the line itself in `ax.lines`.
`scatterplot` puts every point in one collection: `ax.collections[0].get_offsets()` holds the exact (x, y) pairs; `hue` adds a legend, not extra collections.
`histplot(bins=[e0, e1, ...])` bins are half-open `[ei, ei+1)` — a value equal to an edge lands in the bin to its right — except the last bin, which includes its right edge.
`stat='count'` keeps raw counts; `multiple='stack'` piles hue levels, and `ax.patches` lists the bottom layer's bars first.
`relplot`/`displot` are figure-level: they return a `FacetGrid` (use `.figure`), unlike axes-level functions that return the `Axes`.

blocks.title: relplot / scatterplot / lineplot / displot / histplot / kdeplot
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
tips = sns.load_dataset("tips")
penguins = sns.load_dataset("penguins")

# ── scatterplot() ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig,ax = plt.subplots()
sns.scatterplot(data=tips, x="total_bill", y="tip",
    hue="smoker",        # color by column
    size="size",         # marker size by column
    style="time",        # marker shape by column
    palette="Set2",
    alpha=0.8,
    ax=ax)
plt.close()

# ── lineplot() ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig,ax = plt.subplots()
sns.lineplot(data=tips, x="size", y="total_bill",
    hue="time",
    estimator="mean",    # aggregate function
    errorbar=("ci",95),  # confidence interval (or "sd","se","pi")
    markers=True,
    dashes=True,
    ax=ax)
plt.close()

# ── relplot() — figure-level creates FacetGrid ────────────────────
g = sns.relplot(data=tips, x="total_bill", y="tip",
    hue="smoker",
    col="time",          # separate column per time value
    row=None,
    kind="scatter",      # "scatter" or "line"
    col_wrap=None,       # wrap columns after N
    height=4, aspect=1.2,
    palette="colorblind",
)
plt.close()

# ── histplot() ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig,ax = plt.subplots()
sns.histplot(data=tips, x="total_bill",
    hue="smoker",
    bins=20,
    stat="count",        # "count" "frequency" "probability" "percent" "density"
    multiple="dodge",    # "layer" "dodge" "stack" "fill"
    kde=True,            # overlay KDE curve
    element="bars",      # "bars" "step" "poly"
    fill=True,
    alpha=0.6,
    ax=ax)
plt.close()

# ── kdeplot() ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig,ax = plt.subplots()
sns.kdeplot(data=tips, x="total_bill", y="tip",
    hue="smoker",
    fill=True,           # filled contours
    alpha=0.5,
    bw_adjust=0.8,       # >1=smoother <1=rougher (bw_method="scott" default)
    levels=5,            # contour levels (int or list of probs)
    thresh=0.05,         # remove regions below 5% density
    gridsize=100,
    ax=ax)
plt.close()

print("Relational and distribution plots documented")

concepts.title: Categorical Plots
concepts.intro: catplot() is the figure-level wrapper for all categorical plots. kind= selects the specific plot type: box, violin, bar, strip, swarm, point, count, boxen.
concepts.explanation: Categorical plots put one variable on a *category* axis, and seaborn offers a whole family of them. `countplot` is the simplest: it counts rows per category, so bar heights are literally `value_counts()`. `barplot` is subtler: it **aggregates** the `y` column per category with an `estimator` (default `'mean'`, but any callable like `np.median` works) and by default adds a bootstrapped confidence band — pass `errorbar=None` to drop it (the old `ci=` spelling is deprecated). Category order is a real parameter: without `order=` / `hue_order=`, seaborn uses order of *appearance*, which is rarely the order a report wants. `boxplot`, `violinplot`, `stripplot` and `swarmplot` show full distributions instead of single statistics — a box is one patch plus six line artists (whiskers, caps, median). Everything above is axes-level and returns the Axes; `catplot(kind=...)` is the figure-level wrapper that returns a `FacetGrid`. Two 0.13-era facts worth memorizing: grouped bars are stored in `ax.containers` as one `BarContainer` per hue level (the cleanest way to read heights back), and passing `palette` without a `hue` mapping is deprecated. The exercises below have you build a tally and a median bar report and read their bars back exactly.
keyPoints: `countplot` bar heights equal the row counts per category — `[p.get_height() for p in ax.patches]` reads them off in axis order.
`barplot` aggregates `y` per category using `estimator` (default `'mean'`); pass `np.median` for outlier-proof bars and `errorbar=None` to skip the CI band.
Without `order=` / `hue_order=`, categories follow order of appearance in the data — pass explicit lists to control the axis.
With `hue`, seaborn 0.13 stores one `BarContainer` per hue level in `ax.containers`; heights inside a container follow the x-category order.
Passing `palette` without assigning `hue` is deprecated in seaborn 0.13.
`catplot(kind='count'|'bar'|'box'|...)` is figure-level and returns a `FacetGrid`, unlike the axes-level functions that return the `Axes`.

blocks.title: catplot / boxplot / violinplot / barplot / stripplot / swarmplot / countplot
blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
tips = sns.load_dataset("tips")

# ── boxplot() ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig,ax=plt.subplots()
sns.boxplot(data=tips,x="day",y="total_bill",
    hue="smoker",
    order=["Thur","Fri","Sat","Sun"],
    palette="Set3",
    dodge=True,          # separate boxes per hue
    width=0.6,
    whis=1.5,            # IQR multiplier for whiskers
    flierprops=dict(marker="o",markerfacecolor="red",ms=4),
    notch=False,
    showmeans=True,
    meanprops=dict(marker="D",markerfacecolor="white"),
    ax=ax)
plt.close()

# ── violinplot() ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig,ax=plt.subplots()
sns.violinplot(data=tips,x="day",y="total_bill",
    hue="smoker",
    split=True,        # mirror halves per hue
    inner="box",       # "box" "quart" "point" "stick" None
    scale="width",     # "area" "count" "width"
    bw_adjust=0.8,
    palette="muted",
    ax=ax)
plt.close()

# ── barplot() ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig,ax=plt.subplots()
sns.barplot(data=tips,x="day",y="total_bill",
    hue="sex",
    estimator="mean",  # any function: "mean" "median" "sum" np.mean
    errorbar=("ci",95),
    capsize=0.1,
    palette="pastel",
    ax=ax)
plt.close()

# ── countplot() ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig,ax=plt.subplots()
sns.countplot(data=tips,x="day",
    hue="smoker",
    order=tips["day"].value_counts().index,
    dodge=True,
    palette="Set1",
    ax=ax)
plt.close()

# ── stripplot + swarmplot ─────────────────────────────────────────
fig,(a1,a2)=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(10,4))
sns.stripplot(data=tips,x="day",y="total_bill",hue="smoker",
    dodge=True,jitter=0.2,alpha=0.7,size=4,ax=a1)
sns.swarmplot(data=tips,x="day",y="total_bill",hue="smoker",
    dodge=True,size=3,ax=a2)  # no overlap — slow for large N
plt.close()

print("Categorical plots documented")

concepts.title: Matrix & Regression Plots
concepts.intro: heatmap() shows 2D data as colored cells. clustermap() adds hierarchical clustering. lmplot() combines scatter with regression fit and FacetGrid.
concepts.explanation: `sns.heatmap()` paints a 2D matrix as colored cells and is the fastest way to inspect a pivot table or correlation matrix. Its parameters do real work: `annot=True` writes the cell values as text artists (collected in `ax.texts`, row-major), `fmt` controls their formatting (`'d'` for ints, `'.1f'` for one decimal, `'.2%'` for percentages), `vmin`/`vmax` pin the color scale — readable back through `ax.collections[0].get_clim()` — `cbar=False` suppresses the colorbar (which otherwise adds a second axes to the figure), and `mask` hides cells: a `True` cell disappears from both the mesh and the annotation, which is how you show only the lower triangle of a symmetric matrix. For regression, `regplot` is the axes-level workhorse: it draws the scatter plus a fitted line; its current `ci` parameter (`ci=None`) drops the confidence band, leaving exactly one `Line2D` in `ax.lines` and the points in a single scatter collection. `lmplot` is the figure-level sibling — it returns a `FacetGrid` (use `.figure`), splits data across facets with `col=`/`row=`, and titles each facet like `'region = west'`. Beyond those, `clustermap` adds hierarchical clustering dendrograms, `pairplot`/`PairGrid` draw all pairwise relationships, and `jointplot` couples a central plot with marginal distributions. The exercises below build one `regplot` and one masked, annotated heatmap and assert their exact structure.
keyPoints: `heatmap(annot=True)` adds one text per cell to `ax.texts` in row-major order; `fmt='.1f'` renders 0.9 as `'0.9'`.
`vmin`/`vmax` fix the color scale; read them back with `ax.collections[0].get_clim()`.
`mask=True` cells are dropped from the mesh AND the annotation — masking the upper triangle leaves only lower-triangle values.
`cbar=False` keeps the figure at a single axes; the default colorbar adds a second one.
`regplot` returns the Axes with the fitted line in `ax.lines` and the points in a scatter collection; `ci=None` removes the CI band collection.
`lmplot` is figure-level: it returns a `FacetGrid`; `g.axes[0, 1].get_title()` reads the second column facet's title.

blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

sns.set_theme(style="white")

# ── heatmap() ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
flights = sns.load_dataset("flights").pivot(
    index="month",columns="year",values="passengers")
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(10,6))
sns.heatmap(flights,
    annot=True,         # show values in cells
    fmt="d",            # int format ("d" ".1f" ".2%")
    cmap="YlOrRd",
    linewidths=0.5,
    linecolor="white",
    vmin=flights.min().min(),
    vmax=flights.max().max(),
    mask=None,          # bool DataFrame — mask=True hides cell
    square=False,
    cbar=True,
    ax=ax)
plt.close()

# ── clustermap() ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Hierarchical clustering of rows and columns
g=sns.clustermap(flights,
    method="average",    # linkage: "single" "complete" "average" "ward"
    metric="euclidean",  # distance: "euclidean" "correlation" "cosine"
    z_score=0,           # 0=rows 1=cols None=no z-score
    standard_scale=None, # 0=rows 1=cols
    figsize=(10,10),
    cmap="mako",
)
plt.close()

# ── lmplot() — figure-level scatter + regression ───────────────────
tips=sns.load_dataset("tips")
g=sns.lmplot(data=tips,x="total_bill",y="tip",
    hue="smoker",
    col="time",
    fit_reg=True,        # draw regression line
    order=1,             # polynomial order
    ci=95,               # confidence interval
    scatter_kws={"alpha":0.6,"s":30},
    line_kws={"lw":2},
    height=4,aspect=1,
)
plt.close()

# ── regplot() — axes-level ────────────────────────────────────────
fig,ax=plt.subplots()
sns.regplot(data=tips,x="total_bill",y="tip",
    order=1,             # 1=linear 2=quadratic etc
    ci=95,
    robust=False,        # True=LOWESS robust regression
    logistic=False,      # True=logistic for binary y
    ax=ax)
plt.close()

# ── pairplot() ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
penguins=sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna()
g=sns.pairplot(penguins,
    hue="species",
    diag_kind="kde",     # "auto" "hist" "kde" None
    kind="scatter",      # "scatter" "kde" "hist" "reg"
    corner=True,         # show only lower triangle
    markers=["o","s","D"],
    plot_kws={"alpha":0.6,"s":20},
    diag_kws={"fill":True},
)
plt.close()

# ── jointplot() ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
g=sns.jointplot(data=tips,x="total_bill",y="tip",
    kind="reg",          # "scatter" "kde" "hist" "hex" "reg" "resid"
    marginal_ticks=True,
    height=6,ratio=5,    # ratio=size of central vs marginal
)
plt.close()
print("Matrix and regression plots documented")

concepts.title: Color Palettes & Utilities
concepts.intro: color_palette() returns a list of RGB colors. Seaborn's utility functions let you refine figure appearance after plotting.
concepts.explanation: `sns.color_palette()` is the gateway to seaborn's color system: it returns a list of RGB tuples you can pass anywhere a palette is accepted. There are three families. **Qualitative** palettes (`'deep'`, `'pastel'`, `'bright'`, `'muted'`, `'colorblind'`, `'tab10'`) color unordered categories. **Sequential** palettes (`'crest'`, `'flare'`, `'mako'`, `'Blues'`) encode ordered magnitudes — `color_palette('crest', n)` resamples the colormap to exactly `n` evenly spaced colors, and asking for a single color returns the colormap's midpoint. **Diverging** palettes (`'RdBu'`, `'coolwarm'`) put a midpoint between two hues for data centered on zero. A list of hex strings builds a custom palette in that order — `color_palette(['#0E7C7B', '#E4572E'])` — and `as_cmap=True` returns a continuous `Colormap` instead of a list. When you pass `palette=<list>` to a plot function, hue levels map to colors following `hue_order`, and the legend handles carry those exact colors — `get_markerfacecolor()` on a handle reads one back. Beyond color, seaborn ships post-plot utilities: `despine()` removes the top and right spines (with `offset`/`trim` refinements), `move_legend()` relocates a legend on a figure-level object, and `FacetGrid.set_axis_labels()` / `set_titles()` polish multi-panel figures. The exercises below build a gradient programmatically and prove a brand palette landed on the right hue levels.
keyPoints: `color_palette(name, n)` returns a list of exactly `n` RGB tuples — for a sequential map like `'crest'` they are evenly spaced samples, light to dark.
Qualitative palettes (deep, colorblind, tab10…) suit categories; sequential (crest, Blues) suit ordered data; diverging (RdBu, coolwarm) suits values around a midpoint.
`color_palette(['#hex', ...])` builds a custom palette from hex codes in that order; `as_cmap=True` returns a continuous Colormap instead of a list.
Passing `palette=<list>` maps hue levels to colors following `hue_order` — a legend handle's `get_markerfacecolor()` reads the mapped color back.
`sns.despine()` hides the top and right spines by default; left and bottom stay visible.
`move_legend(obj, loc)` and FacetGrid's `set_axis_labels` / `set_titles` refine figures after plotting.

blocks.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# ── color_palette() ──────────────────────────────────────────────
# Qualitative (discrete categories)
q = sns.color_palette("deep")    # 10 colors — default seaborn
q = sns.color_palette("pastel")  # muted pastels
q = sns.color_palette("bright")  # vivid
q = sns.color_palette("muted")   # desaturated
q = sns.color_palette("dark")    # dark
q = sns.color_palette("colorblind")  # 6 CB-safe colors
q = sns.color_palette("tab10")   # matplotlib's tab10

# Sequential (ordered single hue)
s = sns.color_palette("Blues",n_colors=8)
s = sns.color_palette("flare")
s = sns.color_palette("crest")
s = sns.color_palette("mako")

# Diverging (two-hue around center)
d = sns.color_palette("RdBu",n_colors=11)
d = sns.color_palette("coolwarm",as_cmap=True)

# Custom palette
custom = sns.color_palette(["#2196F3","#FF5722","#4CAF50"])
with sns.color_palette(custom):   # context manager
    fig,ax=plt.subplots()
    ax.plot([1,2,3],[1,4,9])
    ax.plot([1,2,3],[2,3,8])
    ax.plot([1,2,3],[3,6,5])
plt.close()

# ── Post-plot utilities ───────────────────────────────────────────
fig,ax=plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1,2,3],[1,4,9])
ax.legend(["data"],loc="upper right")

sns.despine(fig=fig,ax=ax,
    top=True,right=True,   # remove top/right spines
    left=False,bottom=False,
    offset=5,              # shift remaining spines outward
    trim=True,             # trim to data range
)

# move_legend (seaborn 0.12+)
import seaborn as sns2
tips=sns2.load_dataset("tips")
g=sns2.relplot(data=tips,x="total_bill",y="tip",hue="smoker")
sns2.move_legend(g,"lower right",
    bbox_to_anchor=(1,0),
    frameon=True,title="Smoker?")
plt.close()

# ── FacetGrid ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
tips=sns.load_dataset("tips")
import numpy as np
g=sns.FacetGrid(tips,col="time",row="smoker",
    hue="sex",
    height=3,aspect=1.2,
    margin_titles=True,
    palette="Set1",
)
g.map_dataframe(sns.scatterplot,x="total_bill",y="tip",alpha=0.6)
g.add_legend()
g.set_axis_labels("Total Bill ($)","Tip ($)")
g.set_titles(col_template="{col_name}",row_template="{row_name}")
plt.close()

print("All palettes and utilities documented")
print(f"Built-in qualitative palettes: deep,pastel,bright,muted,dark,colorblind,tab10")
